content: The studies listed were excluded for various reasons, primarily because they did not specifically examine the effects of continued breastfeeding as defined by the inclusion criteria. Below is a detailed explanation of the reasons for exclusion for each study: 1. Bloss (2004): This study did not investigate continued breastfeeding beyond 12 months. It focused on the introduction of complementary foods before 6 months as a risk factor. 2. Bobrow (2013): Continued breastfeeding was not studied as defined. Breastfeeding durations analyzed were less than 6 months, 6–9 months, and more than 10 months. 3. Boucher (2017): This study did not compare continued breastfeeding with shorter durations. It analyzed the effects of breastfeeding duration on child development, ADHD, and autism using regression analyses. 4. Bravo (1997): Continued breastfeeding was not studied. The study compared exclusive breastfeeding for less than 4 months versus more than 4 months. 5. Briend (1989): No control group was included. The study compared breastfed versus non-breastfed children aged 12–35 months without details on breastfeeding duration for weaned children. 6. Brinton (1995): This was a case-control study with cases selected from hospital admissions and registries, not representative of the general population. 7. Brion (2011): Continued breastfeeding was not studied. Breastfeeding durations analyzed were less than 1 month, 1–3 months, 3–5 months, and 6 months or more. 8. Brun (1995): Data were not presented in a way that satisfied inclusion criteria. Lactation durations analyzed were 1–9 months, 10–19 months, and more than 20 months. 9. Bulbul (2008): Continued breastfeeding was not studied. Feeding habits were analyzed monthly during the first 6 months, including exclusive breastfeeding, mixed feeding, and formula feeding. 10. Buyken (2008): Continued breastfeeding was not studied. The study used a cutoff of more than 4 months, based on German recommendations for complementary food introduction. 11. Byrne (2018): Continued breastfeeding was not studied. The study focused on exclusive breastfeeding for less than or more than 6 months. 12.
